passage:
Dear Santosh,
I stayed with you for three weeks, and I want to write down something I noticed before I forget. Every evening Meenal told you where she was going, and every evening she was home when she said. She called when the bus was late on Tuesday. She even texted you a photo of the library board, without being asked. These are small things. But I watched them add up, day after day. I don't think you see it, because you're looking for the next mistake. Tell her you've noticed. I saw her face when I said, "Well done for calling, beta." She lit up. Kids keep doing what gets seen.
Your brother,
Lalit

qa.q: What did Meenal text Santosh without being asked?
qa.a: She texted a photo of the library board.

qa.q: Why does Lalit think Santosh hasn't noticed Meenal's progress?
qa.a: He believes Santosh is looking for the next mistake, so the small promises kept each day go unseen.

qa.q: What does Lalit suggest Santosh do?
qa.a: Tell Meenal directly that the kept promises have been noticed, since being seen for honesty encourages more of it.

qa.q: How did Meenal react when Lalit praised her for calling?
qa.a: Her face lit up, showing how much it meant to her that someone noticed.

grounding: Shows a relative noticing a teen keep small promises for weeks and urging the parent to say so aloud, since being noticed encourages honesty.

passage:
I'm Jagdish, Pema's uncle. I stay with them on weekends when I come down from Gangtok.
For six weeks now, I've watched Pema do small things. Every Saturday she tells her mother where she's going before she leaves. She's home when she says she will be. Last Sunday she even texted from the bus, "Running ten minutes late."
My sister hasn't noticed. She's still waiting for the next lie.
So last night I said to her, over dinner, "Pema has kept every promise for six weeks. I've been counting."
Pema looked up from her plate, surprised. My sister looked at her for a long moment. Then she said, "You're right. Thank you, Pema."
Pema smiled all through the dishes.

qa.q: How many weeks had Pema kept her promises?
qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he watched Pema's small actions?
qa.a: Jagdish felt proud and encouraged by Pema's reliability, and eager for her mother to see it.

qa.q: What difference did Jagdish's words make?
qa.a: By noting Pema's track record aloud, Jagdish helped her mother notice the pattern of honesty, which makes more honesty likely.

qa.q: What was Pema experiencing when her mother thanked her?
qa.a: She felt surprised and happy, smiling all through the dishes because her honesty had been noticed.

grounding: An uncle observes his niece keep small promises for weeks and says so aloud to her mother, helping honesty be noticed.

Week one: Afreen, visiting her sister's family for the summer, noticed her niece Gopika always said where she was going now. "Library till five, Khala." And she was home by five.
Week three: Gopika texted her mother before leaving tuition, every single day. Afreen saw her sister still frowning at the phone, checking.
Week five: At dinner, Afreen said, "Gopika has told you the truth about every plan for five weeks. I've been watching." Her sister looked up. Gopika froze, fork in the air.
Her sister said slowly, "I suppose she has." Then, to Gopika, "Thank you." Gopika grinned so wide she almost dropped the fork.

qa.q: What did Gopika call Afreen?
qa.a: Khala.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she saw her sister still frowning at the phone?
qa.a: Afreen felt concerned that her sister wasn't noticing Gopika's efforts.

qa.q: Why did Afreen's words at dinner matter?
qa.a: Afreen pointed out the pattern of five weeks of honesty, helping her sister see the track record and making Gopika more likely to keep it up.

qa.q: What was Gopika experiencing when her mother thanked her?
qa.a: She felt surprised and delighted, grinning widely at being recognised for her honesty.

grounding: An aunt notices her niece keep small promises over weeks and points it out to the mother, helping trust show up in ordinary days.

passage:
Suraj, you want to know how your Papa and your Dadi became close again when he was your age? I'll tell you. I'm Anand, his mama, and I saw it.
Your Papa, at fifteen, had lied about a cricket match in another town. Your Dadi stopped believing anything he said.
That summer I stayed with them. And I watched. Every day he said where he was going. Every evening he was home on time. He even told her when he broke a glass.
After a month, I said to your Dadi, "He's kept every word for four weeks. Have you noticed?" She hadn't. She looked at him, surprised.
He stood up straighter after that. He kept being honest, because now someone was noticing.

qa.q: What had Suraj's Papa lied about at fifteen?
qa.a: A cricket match in another town.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling as he watched his nephew that summer?
qa.a: Anand felt proud and hopeful, seeing his nephew keep his word every day.

qa.q: In the story, what was the turning point?
qa.a: When Anand pointed out the four-week track record to Suraj's Dadi, she finally noticed, and being noticed made the boy even more honest.

qa.q: What was Suraj's Papa experiencing when his mother looked at him surprised?
qa.a: He likely felt seen and encouraged, standing up straighter because his honesty had been recognised.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing his nephew keep small promises for weeks and pointing it out to the boy's mother, helping trust return.

The wedding week was chaos. Forty relatives in one house in Lucknow, power cuts every evening, and Hafsa Mami watching everything from the kitchen door.

She knew about Pankaj's lie in the spring, and the new rules after. She'd been skeptical.

But on Monday, when the lights went out, Pankaj texted his mother: "At the tent house with Nitin, back by 8." He was back at 7:50. On Wednesday, asked to fetch sweets, he returned with the change and the bill. On Friday, he told his mother before going to the terrace with his cousins, though nobody would have noticed.

Hafsa found his mother alone, folding saris. "Your boy has kept every small promise this week. In all this madness. I've been counting."

His mother looked up, surprised. Across the courtyard, Pankaj heard, and pretended he hadn't. But he stood a little straighter.

qa.q: What time did Pankaj get back on Monday?
qa.a: He was back at 7:50.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling as she watched Pankaj through the week?
qa.a: She started out skeptical but grew impressed and warm as she saw him keep every small promise.

qa.q: Why was it useful for Hafsa to say it aloud to his mother?
qa.a: Naming his honesty helped his mother see the pattern of ordinary days, and being noticed made Pankaj more likely to keep it up.

qa.q: How is Pankaj affected when he overhears Hafsa?
qa.a: He pretends not to hear but stands straighter, suggesting he feels proud and encouraged.

grounding: During a hectic wedding week a relative notices a teen keeping small promises and tells the parent, showing trust built through ordinary days.
